segments.voice: Last week ended in the Devi Mahatmya with one syllable, hum, and Kali springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda. Did you stand up for something, firmly and without cruelty? A new week. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

Every drop. That's the problem in the eighth chapter. Shumbha, his generals dead, sends out his whole army. And to meet it, something new happens. From the bodies of the gods, their powers step out, each one a goddess in that god's own form. From Brahma, a goddess on a swan, with prayer beads and a water pot. From Shiva, one on a bull, holding a trident. From Vishnu, one on Garuda, the great bird. From Indra, one with a thunderbolt, on an elephant. A boar-faced goddess. A lion-faced goddess. They surround the goddess on the battlefield. And then a demon walks out to meet them, named Raktabija. Blood-Seed.
screen: `SHUMBHA SENDS HIS WHOLE ARMY.` → `THE GODS' POWERS STEP OUT.` → `A DEMON NAMED BLOOD-SEED.`

segments.voice: First, though, the goddess does something surprising. From her own body comes one more power, fierce, howling like a pack of jackals, and she gives Shiva himself a job: go to Shumbha and Nishumbha as my messenger. Tell them to give heaven back and go home to the underworld, or come and fight. Because she sent Shiva as her messenger, she's called Shivaduti, the one whose messenger is Shiva. The demons choose to fight. Then Raktabija. His power is in his name. Whenever a drop of his blood falls to the ground, a new demon rises from it, just as strong as he is. The goddesses strike him with thunderbolt, spear, discus, trident. And each wound makes it worse. Drops fall, and from every drop, another Raktabija. Soon the whole field is full of him. The gods are terrified. Here's the move the text makes. The goddess, smiling, turns to Kali and says, in paraphrase: open your mouth wide. Take in every drop of blood before it touches the ground. So Kali does. As the goddess strikes, Kali drinks the blood, and swallows the new demons as they rise. The drops stop landing. Raktabija weakens, drained, and at last he falls. Notice what wins here. Not a bigger weapon. Every weapon only made more of him. What wins is not letting the drops land: catching the thing before it can grow again. Some readers hear in Raktabija the way a resentment or a craving multiplies each time it's fed. The text leaves that open. What it shows is Kali's open mouth, and a field that finally empties.
screen: `SHIVA SENT AS HER MESSENGER.` · `EVERY DROP BECOMES A DEMON.` · `EACH WOUND MAKES IT WORSE.` · `KALI CATCHES EVERY DROP.` · then, large: `DON'T LET THE DROPS LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch the drop. Settle, and let the breath slow. Let a small irritation come to mind, nothing huge. Watch what happens when you think about it: one thought, and then another grows from it, and another. That's the multiplying. Now, gently, go back to the first one. Just the first. Don't feed it, don't fight it. Breathe it in, and on the breath out, let it settle, before it can land and grow. If it multiplies again, come back again. If you pray, you can ask for help in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath be what catches it. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its eighth chapter: the gods' powers as goddesses, Shiva sent as a messenger, and Raktabija, beaten when Kali caught every drop.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when one annoyed thought starts making more, catch the first one, and let it go before it lands. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The goddesses who come out of the gods in the eighth chapter are known together as the Matrikas, the Mothers, and groups of them are carved and worshiped in some Hindu temples.

original.note: Sanskrit: rakta-bīja, blood-seed. The demon whose every drop of blood becomes another of him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gory battle story.
what it means: a demon who multiplies every time he's wounded, beaten only when the drops are caught before they land.
what a scholar hears: chapter 8, with the śaktis of the gods (the Mātṛkās), the goddess as Śivadūtī, and Kālī drinking Raktabīja's blood.

notes: First day of week two of year four. Chapter 8 paraphrased: the śaktis of Brahma (on a swan, rosary and water pot), Maheshvara (on a bull, trident), Kumara (peacock, spear; not named in the voice), Vishnu (on Garuda), Varahi (boar form), Narasimhi (lion form), Indra (thunderbolt, on Airavata). The text names more forms; the script names some. Confirm.
Chandika's own śakti, howling like jackals, sends Shiva as messenger (give back the three worlds and go to Pātāla, or fight); hence Śivadūtī. Confirm.
Raktabija: each drop of blood falling to earth produces an asura equal to him; Kali drinks the blood and devours the new ones; he falls bloodless. Confirm.
'Some readers hear in Raktabija the way a resentment or a craving multiplies' is attributed interpretation; confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
howItsDone: 'Matrikas' as the group name and temple worship of them; confirm.
